cues.en: I make videos about walkable cities and urban mobility.
cues.zh: 我做关于步行友好城市和城市交通的视频。

cues.en: I mostly talk about great cities in Europe, so as you'd expect, I get a lot of excuses and cope, especially from North Americans.
cues.zh: 我主要讲欧洲的优秀城市，所以如你所料，我听到很多借口和嘴硬，尤其来自北美人。

cues.en: Now, I'm not particularly interested in making debunking videos.
cues.zh: 不过，我对做辟谣视频没太大兴趣。

cues.en: I'd rather show you examples of great cities and let my experiences
cues.zh: 我更愿意给你看优秀城市的例子，让我的经历

cues.en: speak for themselves.
cues.zh: 自己说话。

cues.en: But there's one lame excuse that is so common,
cues.zh: 但有一个烂借口太常见了，

cues.en: so prevalent,
cues.zh: 太普遍了，

cues.en: so ubiquitous
cues.zh: 太泛滥了，

cues.en: that I want to talk about it.
cues.zh: 以至于我想专门谈谈它。

cues.en: And that's the excuse that my country is too big to have trains, bicycle infrastructure,
cues.zh: 这就是那个借口：我的国家太大了，没法拥有火车、自行车基础设施，

cues.en: walkable neighborhoods or whatever.
cues.zh: 适合步行的社区之类的。

cues.en: This is an excellent and well thought out explanation as to why North American cities are so terrible. Well, that is until you think about it for more than about twelve seconds.
cues.zh: 这是关于北美城市为何如此糟糕的一个出色且深思熟虑的解释。嗯，前提是你别多想超过大约十二秒。

cues.en: Most people are ignorant about urban planning and urban mobility. I certainly was until about a decade ago. And that's understandable.
cues.zh: 大多数人对城市规划和城市出行并不了解。大约十年前的我绝对也是这样。而这可以理解。

cues.en: I mean, why would you know about these things? Right? But Americans are uniquely ignorant because American cities are very poorly designed, and their insular culture and limited international travel opportunities means that most Americans have never even seen a well designed city.
cues.zh: 我是说，你怎么会懂这些呢？对吧？但美国人的无知是独一份的，因为美国城市设计得很糟，加上他们封闭的文化和有限的出国旅行机会，大多数美国人甚至从没见过一座设计良好的城市。

cues.en: Though, to be fair, Canadians and Australians aren't very far behind.
cues.zh: 不过说句公道话，加拿大人和澳大利亚人也差不了多少。

cues.en: So when someone new to walkable cities sees an example of a great city and they realize it clearly better than where they live, their first gut reaction is to grab any difference between the two and make that the reason as to why their city can't be the same.
cues.zh: 所以，当一个刚接触步行城市的人看到一座优秀城市的范例，意识到它明显比自己住的地方更好时，他们的第一反应就是抓住两者之间的任何差异，把它当成自己城市没法变成那样的理由。

cues.en: Sometimes it's the weather, Canadians love that one.
cues.zh: 有时候是天气，加拿大人最爱说这个。

cues.en: Sometimes it's culture,
cues.zh: 有时候是文化，

cues.en: sometimes it's population,
cues.zh: 有时候是人口，

cues.en: sometimes it's a misunderstanding of history.
cues.zh: 有时候是对历史的误解。

cues.en: But usually, it's that European country is small, my country is big, this video is stupid, and you're an idiot, or something along those lines.
cues.zh: 但通常，是那个欧洲国家很小、我们国家很大、这视频很蠢、你是个白痴，诸如此类的话。

cues.en: My personal favorite though is the Wikipedia
cues.zh: 不过我个人最喜欢的，是维基百科

cues.en: contrarian.
cues.zh: 杠精。

cues.en: That guy who looks up the size of The Netherlands on Google or Wikipedia,
cues.zh: 就是那种去谷歌或维基百科查荷兰面积的人，

cues.en: and then paste that number into their comment like it's some kind of epic own.
cues.zh: 然后把那个数字贴进评论里，好像这是什么惊天反击似的。

cues.en: And I can tell which source they use because Wikipedia and Google have different numbers.
cues.zh: 而且我能看出他们用的是哪个来源，因为维基百科和谷歌给出的数字不一样。

cues.en: In case you're curious, here's how big The Netherlands is compared to The United States, Canada, and Australia.
cues.zh: 如果你好奇的话，这是荷兰相对于美国、加拿大和澳大利亚的面积对比。

cues.en: So why is this argument so stupid?
cues.zh: 那为什么这个论点这么蠢呢？

cues.en: Well, quite simply,
cues.zh: 很简单，

cues.en: Americans aren't traveling from Fluffy Landing to Hump Tulips every day. Canadians aren't traveling from Dildo to Spuzzum every day. And Australians aren't travelling from Chinaman's Knob to Useless Loop everyday.
cues.zh: 美国人不会每天从 Fluffy Landing 通勤到 Hump Tulips，加拿大人不会每天从 Dildo 通勤到 Spuzzum，澳大利亚人也不会每天从 Chinaman's Knob 通勤到 Useless Loop。

cues.en: And also, why are there two places in Australia called Chinaman's Knob? Alright. You know what? I am done talking about Australia.
cues.zh: 还有，为什么澳大利亚有两个地方都叫 Chinaman's Knob？好吧。你知道吗？我不再聊澳大利亚了。

cues.en: People do not travel across their country on a regular basis. They travel within their city. So the only thing that really matters to most people is the design of that city,
cues.zh: 人们并不会经常横跨整个国家出行。他们是在自己城市里活动。所以对大多数人来说，真正重要的只有这座城市的设计，

cues.en: which is what we're talking about here.
cues.zh: 而这正是我们在这里要谈的。

cues.en: For example, in The United States,
cues.zh: 举个例子，在美国，

cues.en: over 45%
cues.zh: 超过 45%

cues.en: of trips, all trips,
cues.zh: 的出行，所有出行中，

cues.en: are three miles or less. That's five kilometers for the rest of my audience.
cues.zh: 都在三英里以内。对我的其他听众来说，就是五公里。

cues.en: These are distances that could be easily done by walking or cycling.
cues.zh: 这些距离步行或骑车就能轻松搞定。

cues.en: So despite the size of the country and the sprawliness of the cities, Americans don't actually travel that far for most trips.
cues.zh: 所以，尽管国家幅员辽阔、城市不断向外摊开，美国人大多数出行其实并不会走那么远。

cues.en: But unsurprisingly,
cues.zh: 但不出所料，

cues.en: almost all of those trips are taken by car because it's too dangerous to walk or cycle and public transportation is non existent,
cues.zh: 几乎所有这类出行都是开车，因为步行或骑车太危险，公共交通又根本不存在，

cues.en: which again is the whole point.
cues.zh: 而这恰恰就是关键所在。

cues.en: This may come as a surprise to some people because Americans are obsessed with commuting and the average commute length in The US is about 20 miles. That's 32 kilometers for everyone else.
cues.zh: 有些人可能会感到意外，因为美国人对通勤很有执念，而美国的平均通勤距离约为20英里。换成公制就是32公里。

cues.en: But there are many more trips that people take on a daily basis that are not commuting.
cues.zh: 但人们每天还有更多出行并不是通勤。

cues.en: Even here in The Netherlands, there are many places, especially smaller towns and villages, where people commute to work by car.
cues.zh: 即使在荷兰，也有许多地方，尤其是小城镇和村庄，人们开车通勤。

cues.en: But do all of their other trips such as grocery shopping, visiting friends, or going to appointments by walking, cycling, or public transit.
cues.zh: 但他们的其他出行，比如买菜、访友或赴约，是否都靠步行、骑行或公共交通呢？

cues.en: They have those options available to them for shorter trips, which again
cues.zh: 对于较短距离的出行，他们也有这些选择，而这又

cues.en: is the point.
cues.zh: 正是关键所在。

cues.en: The problem is not cars,
cues.zh: 问题不在汽车，

cues.en: it's car dependency.
cues.zh: 而在于对汽车的依赖。

cues.en: We need to give people the freedom to not to have to drive.
cues.zh: 我们得让人们拥有不必开车的自由。

cues.en: Though regardless,
cues.zh: 不过话说回来，

cues.en: 32 kilometers is still a perfectly reasonable distance to commute by train if those trains existed.
cues.zh: 32 公里仍然是非常合理的火车通勤距离——前提是得有那些火车。

cues.en: And now this is where Americans will claim that America is too big for trains which is absolutely
cues.zh: 这时候美国人就会说，美国太大了，不适合火车，这简直

cues.en: comical because
cues.zh: 很可笑，因为

cues.en: America was literally built by the railroads and so was Canada for that matter.
cues.zh: 美国确实就是靠铁路建起来的，加拿大也一样。

cues.en: In the eighteen hundreds, a railroad company would buy up all the land west of wherever they were, build a railroad and a bunch of stations, and then sell the land near those stations made valuable by the rail line to recoup their investment.
cues.zh: 在19世纪，铁路公司会把铁路线以西的所有土地买下来，修建铁路和一批车站，然后出售因铁路而升值的车站附近土地，以收回投资。

cues.en: Nearly every town, city, and village in The United States and Canada had a train station and was connected by rail with very few exceptions.
cues.zh: 美国和加拿大几乎每一座城镇、城市和村庄都有火车站，并通过铁路相连，极少例外。

cues.en: And almost every city and town had a streetcar line too with very few exceptions.
cues.zh: 几乎每座城市和城镇也都有有轨电车线路，同样极少例外。

cues.en: And every one of those places was built to be walkable as every one of those places was built before automobiles were common. Again,
cues.zh: 这些地方每一处建造时都适合步行，因为它们都建于汽车普及之前。再说，

cues.en: with very few exceptions.
cues.zh: 只有极少数例外。

cues.en: A hundred years ago, you could get a train from almost any city to just about any other city on the continent and even many towns and villages too.
cues.zh: 一百年前，你几乎可以从这片大陆上任何一座城市坐火车到任何另一座城市，甚至许多城镇和村庄。

cues.en: The reason those train stations don't exist anymore is because they were bulldozed,
cues.zh: 那些火车站如今不复存在，是因为它们被推土机铲平了，

cues.en: often to make room for highways,
cues.zh: 往往是为了给高速公路腾地方，

cues.en: along with the walkable downtowns they were connected to.
cues.zh: 连同它们连接的、适合步行的市中心也一起被铲平了。

cues.en: American cities were not built for the car. They were bulldozed for the car.
cues.zh: 美国城市并非为汽车而建，而是为汽车被推倒重建的。

cues.en: But even if North America wasn't built on trains, and to be clear, it was, the size of the country would still be irrelevant because most intercity travel is still regional.
cues.zh: 但就算北美不是靠铁路建起来的——说清楚点，它确实是——国土面积也依然无关紧要，因为大多数城际出行仍然是区域性的。

cues.en: There are dozens of city pairs in The US that are the perfect population and distance for high speed rail or high frequency rail, and City Nerd has made a video about this if you'd like more details.
cues.zh: 美国有几十对城市，其人口规模和距离都完美适合高铁或高频铁路，City Nerd 做过一期相关视频，想了解更多细节可以去看看。

cues.en: As for Canada, it may be a huge country, but about 50% of the entire population lives in this little area, which is literally in a line.
cues.zh: 至于加拿大，它可能是个大国，但全国约50%的人口都住在这块小区域里，而且真的就排成一条线。

cues.en: And this is Japan to scale, the country famous for all its trains.
cues.zh: 这是按相同比例的日本，一个以列车闻名的国家。

cues.en: So yes, Canada, you can build a high speed train between Toronto and Montreal.
cues.zh: 所以没错，加拿大，你可以在多伦多和蒙特利尔之间建一条高铁。

cues.en: Oh, and by the way, here's China with its high speed rail map.
cues.zh: 哦对了，顺便看看中国的高铁线路图。

cues.en: I always laugh when some ignorant commenter tells me, you obviously have no idea how big The US is. But actually, yes, I know exactly how big it is because I've driven across the continent eight times.
cues.zh: 每当有无知的评论者跟我说“你显然不知道美国有多大”，我总是想笑。但其实，我当然很清楚它有多大，因为我曾八次驾车横穿这片大陆。

cues.en: I know that you can travel long distances in America without encountering any borders, but did you know that you can do that in Europe too?
cues.zh: 我知道在美国长途旅行不会遇到任何边境，但你知道在欧洲也可以吗？

cues.en: This is the Schengen Zone, a group of European countries that allows visa free travel. That means I can drive to any one of these places and never encounter a border at all.
cues.zh: 这就是申根区，一个由允许免签旅行的欧洲国家组成的区域。也就是说，我可以开车去其中任何一个地方，完全不会遇到边境。

cues.en: Yes.
cues.zh: 是的。

cues.en: I know I can't drive to Iceland.
cues.zh: 我知道我不能开车去冰岛。

cues.en: But the Schengen Zone is not constant and new countries are being added every few years. For example, Croatia was just added in 2023.
cues.zh: 但申根区不是固定不变的，每隔几年就会有新国家加入。比如，克罗地亚刚刚在2023年加入。

cues.en: And Bulgaria,
cues.zh: 还有保加利亚，

cues.en: Romania, Cyprus, and Montenegro plan to join in the near future.
cues.zh: 罗马尼亚、塞浦路斯和黑山计划在不久的将来加入。

cues.en: But if that happens, will Amsterdam need to tear up all their bike lanes because the Schengen Zone is too big?
cues.zh: 但若真如此，阿姆斯特丹是否要拆掉所有自行车道，就因为申根区太大？

cues.en: No. Of course not. That would be stupid, which is the same reason why saying America is too big for bike lanes is also stupid.
cues.zh: 不。当然不会。那会很蠢；同理，说美国太大不适合建自行车道也很蠢。

cues.en: The fact is, it is possible to build walkable neighborhoods everywhere.
cues.zh: 事实是，任何地方都可以建设步行友好社区。

cues.en: They have existed in every country on earth for thousands of years.
cues.zh: 它们在地球上每个国家都已存在数千年。

cues.en: And it is possible to connect those walkable places together by high quality public transportation
cues.zh: 通过高质量的公共交通，可以把这些可步行的地方连接起来

cues.en: to make it so that people can go from any walkable area to any other walkable area regardless of the size of the city, the country, or the continent.
cues.zh: 让人们在任何可步行区域之间自由往来，不管城市、国家还是大洲有多大。

cues.en: That's how I can bike to the station in Amsterdam,
cues.zh: 正因如此，我才能骑车到阿姆斯特丹的车站，

cues.en: get on a high speed train to Berlin, transfer to the U Bahn, and walk to my hotel.
cues.zh: 坐上开往柏林的高铁，换乘 U Bahn，再步行到酒店。

cues.en: But even if size did matter, then why isn't Maryland covered in bike lanes and train tracks, or Hawaii,
cues.zh: 但就算Size真的重要，那为什么马里兰州没有遍地自行车道和铁轨，夏威夷也没有，

cues.en: or Prince Edward Island?
cues.zh: 爱德华王子岛也没有？

cues.en: Instead, pretty much everywhere in The US and Canada looks exactly like this
cues.zh: 恰恰相反，美国和加拿大几乎所有地方都长这样

cues.en: regardless of where it is or what size it is.
cues.zh: 不管它在哪儿、规模多大。

cues.en: So why do American cities suck so much then?
cues.zh: 那为什么美国城市还这么糟糕呢？

cues.en: Well, there are lots of reasons as I've talked about in many many previous videos, but I think the most important one to talk about here is bad land use.
cues.zh: 原因有很多，我之前很多视频里都讲过，但我认为这里最该说的是糟糕的土地利用。

cues.en: US and Canadian cities waste land.
cues.zh: 美国和加拿大城市在浪费土地。

cues.en: They use huge amounts of land for single family housing,
cues.zh: 它们把大量土地用于独户住宅、

cues.en: surface parking lots,
cues.zh: 地面停车场、

cues.en: low density developments,
cues.zh: 低密度开发项目，

cues.en: and excessively wide stroads.
cues.zh: 以及宽得离谱的"街路"（stroad）。

cues.en: When you travel around any North American city, you'll see empty lots like this all over the place.
cues.zh: 你在北美任何城市转一圈，都会到处看到这样的空地。

cues.en: There's no acknowledgement that good land is valuable, that it can be used for more efficient purposes.
cues.zh: 没人承认好地皮是有价值的，可以用来做更高效的事。

cues.en: If the local strip mall goes out of business, it isn't turned into something more useful, it's just left there to rot and a new big box store is built farther down the road.
cues.zh: 如果本地的沿街商铺倒闭了，它不会被改造成更有用的东西，就只是扔在那儿烂掉，然后在更远的路边再建一座新的大型仓储式商店。

cues.en: This makes everything too spread out to walk and too inefficient for public transportation
cues.zh: 这让一切都太分散，根本没法步行，对公共交通来说也太低效

cues.en: and it's usually too dangerous to cycle because of all the cars.
cues.zh: 而且因为车太多，骑车通常也太危险。

cues.en: This is ultimately the root of a lot of the problems that I talk about on this channel.
cues.zh: 这归根结底是我在这个频道里谈到的许多问题的根源。

cues.en: In particular, I made the video linked here in the top right about how this explains why public transportation is so bad in North America.
cues.zh: 我专门做了右上角链接的这个视频，讲这如何解释了北美公共交通为何如此糟糕。

cues.en: Now you could argue that a bigger country lets you be lazier with land use. But on the flip side, The Netherlands doesn't have good land use because it's small.
cues.zh: 你可能会说，国家更大，土地规划就可以更松懈。但反过来，荷兰并不是因为国土小才有良好的土地使用。

cues.en: It has good land use because there were policies and regulations put in place to use land efficiently
cues.zh: 它之所以土地使用得好，是因为制定了政策和法规来高效利用土地，

cues.en: in order to protect good quality arable farmland,
cues.zh: 为了保护优质耕地，

cues.en: which is one of the reasons why The Netherlands is the world's second largest exporter of agricultural products by value.
cues.zh: 这也是荷兰成为世界第二大农产品出口国（按价值计）的原因之一。

cues.en: This wasn't an inevitability and there are lots and lots of smaller countries in the world that don't do this right.
cues.zh: 这并非不可避免，世界上有很多很多较小的国家并没有这样做。

cues.en: The United States destroys over 750,000
cues.zh: 美国毁掉超过 75 万

cues.en: acres of natural and agricultural lands every year to build sprawling suburbs.
cues.zh: 英亩的自然和农业用地，每年用来建造不断蔓延的郊区。

cues.en: And Ontario, Canada, where I'm from, destroys a 175 acres of farmland per day
cues.zh: 而在我来自的加拿大安大略省，每天毁掉 175 英亩农田

cues.en: to build more car dependent suburbia.
cues.zh: 来建造更多依赖汽车的郊区。

cues.en: That is a choice.
cues.zh: 这是一种选择。

cues.en: So when Americans say something like US cities are too big and spread out to do whatever, then yes,
cues.zh: 所以当美国人说美国城市太大、太分散，做不了某些事时，那么没错，

cues.en: that's true.
cues.zh: 确实如此。

cues.en: But that is literally the problem that urbanists are trying to solve. So it's not really helpful to restate the problem and then use that as the excuse as to why it can't be solved.
cues.zh: 但这正是城市主义者试图解决的问题。所以，把问题重述一遍，再拿它当作无法解决的借口，其实没什么帮助。

cues.en: Though I admit, actually fixing American and Canadian cities after they were destroyed by car infrastructure and then rebuilt to be car dependent is a very daunting task. And I'm personally not even convinced it can be done in the foreseeable future,
cues.zh: 不过我承认，美国和加拿大城市先被汽车基础设施摧毁，又被重建为依赖汽车的城市，要真正修复它们确实是一项非常艰巨的任务。而且我个人甚至不相信这能在可预见的未来做到，

cues.en: which is a big part of the reason why we left North America for a better city in The Netherlands in the first place.
cues.zh: 这也是我们当初离开北美、搬到荷兰一座更好的城市的主要原因之一。

cues.en: Because ultimately,
cues.zh: 因为归根结底，

cues.en: the Dutch make great places while North Americans
cues.zh: 荷兰人能打造出好地方，而北美人

cues.en: make excuses.
cues.zh: 只会找借口。

cues.en: But there's no excuse for watching ads and sponsor messages on YouTube when you could be watching this video on Nebula.
